_comment: City pages for the major metro cities. Phoenix is intentionally absent: the
home page already targets it. Keep every field specific to its city.
neighborhoods/faqs/nearby feed the page sections and FAQPage schema.

cities.hook: the highest ticket in the Valley.
cities.sub: Scottsdale home improvement searches convert into the largest jobs in the metro — and into the most crowded set of Google Business Profiles anywhere in Arizona.
cities.market: Scottsdale is really two markets wearing one name. South of Camelback the housing stock is mid-century ranch — original aluminium windows, flat and low-slope roofs, kitchens and baths that have been remodelled once since 1975. North of the 101 it is 1990s-and-later custom and semi-custom homes on big lots, where the work is upgrade rather than repair, and where a single job can be worth more than a month of work anywhere else in the Valley.
cities.why: Both halves search the same way — on a phone, from the house, using the map. What changes is the stakes. A frameless enclosure quote in Paradise Valley and one in west Mesa involve the same three-minute search and wildly different invoices, which is why every well-funded contractor in the metro already advertises here. The map pack in Scottsdale is not won on effort; it is won on profile completeness, review recency, and having pages that actually name the neighbourhoods you work in.
cities.trades_why: Luxury remodel trades index hardest here — frameless glass, plantation shutters and motorised shade, high-end windows and doors, and cabinet-grade interior painting.
cities.note: This territory covers Paradise Valley as well. One contractor per trade holds both.
cities.needs_data: Add the three profiles currently holding the Scottsdale map for your trade, and a geo-grid screenshot centred on Old Town.

faqs.q: Do I need a Scottsdale address to rank in Scottsdale?
faqs.a: No, but proximity is still the strongest single factor in the map pack. A shop in Tempe or north Phoenix can rank across much of Scottsdale; ranking in Troon North from a south Tempe address is a much harder ask. The geo-grid shows exactly where your radius currently ends, which is the point of running the free scan before anyone promises you anything.

faqs.q: Why is my competitor outranking me when I have more reviews?
faqs.a: Review count is one input among many, and it is rarely the deciding one in Scottsdale. Category completeness, proximity to the searcher, review recency and how much of your profile is actually filled in all carry weight. A competitor with forty recent reviews and nine service categories will usually beat a hundred reviews from 2021 and two categories.

faqs.q: Is high-end work harder to rank for here?
faqs.a: The searches are not harder, the competition is better funded. Everyone chasing a Paradise Valley remodel budget is already advertising. That is why we lean on the things money cannot shortcut: review velocity after every job, real photography of local work, and pages that name the neighbourhoods you actually serve.

faqs.q: Which trades are still open in Scottsdale?
faqs.a: All eight at the time of writing. Scottsdale and Paradise Valley are sold as one territory, so taking it covers both cities for your trade.

cities.hook: the most houses that need work.
cities.sub: Mesa has more homes that need work than any other city in the metro — and a map pack that most East Valley contractors have never seriously contested.
cities.market: Mesa is the third-largest city in Arizona and, for a home improvement contractor, the most straightforwardly profitable demographic in the metro: a very large stock of houses built between the 1960s and the 1990s, a substantial retiree and winter-visitor population with equity and no mortgage, and a culture of getting three quotes before committing. Original roofs, original windows, and original HVAC are all reaching end of life across whole subdivisions at once.
cities.why: The searches here skew toward repair and replacement rather than aspiration — "roof repair near me", "ac not cooling", "window replacement cost". That intent is immediate and local, which makes the map pack decisive: the homeowner is not researching, they are picking someone to come out this week. Mesa is wide open: we hold no client here in any trade, which is unusual for a city this size and this far into its replacement cycle.
cities.trades_why: Replacement-cycle trades dominate — roofing, HVAC, garage doors, and flooring, in roughly that order of urgency.
cities.note: Every trade is open in this territory, including windows and doors.
cities.needs_data: Mesa is the largest genuinely uncontested territory on the list. A geo-grid scan of one trade here would make the argument concretely.

faqs.q: Is Mesa less competitive than Scottsdale or Chandler?
faqs.a: On the map, yes, and by a wider margin than the size of the city would suggest. Mesa has more homes needing work than anywhere else in the metro and noticeably less complete profile work behind them. That gap is the reason we flag it as the largest genuinely uncontested territory on our list.

faqs.q: Most of my work comes from referrals. Why bother with the map?
faqs.a: Referrals do not scale with your capacity, and they dry up first when the market slows. Map visibility is the channel that keeps producing when the phone stops ringing on its own. It also captures the homeowner who was referred to you but searched your name plus 'reviews' before calling.

faqs.q: My customers are retirees. Do they even use Google Maps?
faqs.a: They use it more than most people assume, usually on a phone handed to them by an adult child helping with the decision. Mesa's winter-visitor and retiree population is also unusually review-driven: they read them carefully and they leave them when asked, which makes review velocity work harder here than almost anywhere in the Valley.

faqs.q: How far does the Mesa territory reach?
faqs.a: Mesa and the East Valley are sold as one territory, which includes Tempe. One contractor per trade holds the whole thing.

cities.sub: Chandler homeowners research harder, compare more, and read reviews more carefully than anywhere else in the Valley. That rewards a complete profile and punishes a thin one.
cities.market: Chandler grew up around the semiconductor industry — Intel's largest Arizona campuses sit here — and the household profile shows it: dual-income, technical, comfortable, and inclined to do homework before spending money. The housing is largely master-planned and built from the late 1980s onward, with the big southern developments now old enough that their original roofs, water heaters and flooring are all coming due at once.
cities.why: The buying behaviour is what matters for search. A Chandler homeowner is more likely to open all three map results, read the one-star reviews first, check whether you replied to them, and look at your photos before calling anyone. That means review volume alone does not win here — review recency, owner responses, and real job photography do. It also means a half-finished profile gets eliminated in the comparison rather than simply ranked lower.
cities.trades_why: Upgrade-cycle trades lead — flooring replacement, first-time re-roofs on 1990s builds, shutters and shade, and garage door replacement.
cities.note: This territory is Chandler and Gilbert together. One contractor per trade covers both cities.
cities.needs_data: Worth pulling the average review count of the current top three here — the comparison-shopping angle is much stronger with a real number attached.

faqs.q: Why do Chandler homeowners take longer to book?
faqs.a: Because they compare more. The household profile here skews technical and dual-income, and the buying pattern shows it: all three map results opened, one-star reviews read first, owner responses checked. That lengthens the decision but it also rewards you, because a complete profile wins a comparison that a thin one never even enters.

faqs.q: Do owner responses to reviews actually matter?
faqs.a: In Chandler more than most places. A measured reply to a bad review is read as evidence of how you handle problems, which is exactly what a comparison shopper is trying to work out. We draft responses within a day, including the unflattering ones.

faqs.q: Is Chandler sold separately from Gilbert?
faqs.a: No. Chandler and Gilbert are one territory, so one contractor per trade covers both cities. It is the densest pair of master-planned suburbs in the metro and splitting them would put two of our own clients in the same map.

faqs.q: What if my Google profile was set up years ago and never touched?
faqs.a: That is the normal starting point, and it is usually the cheapest win available. Most of the first month is category completion, service areas, hours, attributes and photographs, all of which move the map before a single new page is written.

cities.hook: the newest homes are coming due.
cities.sub: Gilbert spent two decades as one of the fastest-growing municipalities in the country. Those homes are now hitting their first replacement cycle, all at once.
cities.market: Gilbert is still officially a town, which is a useful reminder of how recently it was farmland. It went from a few thousand residents to a quarter of a million in a generation, almost entirely as master-planned subdivisions built from the mid-1990s through the 2010s. The consequence for contractors is unusual and specific: an enormous number of near-identical houses of near-identical age, arriving at their first major replacement cycle simultaneously.
cities.why: That creates a wave pattern that rewards visibility more than it rewards capacity. When one street re-roofs or repaints, neighbours follow within the season — and the contractor they find is the one on the map when they search, or the one parked in the neighbour's driveway. Winning the map here is compounding: map visibility produces the first job in a subdivision, and the first job produces the rest of the street. Gilbert is also young and heavily family-skewed, so the interior trades — flooring, paint, shade — move on kids and pets rather than on failure.
cities.trades_why: First-cycle replacement leads — roofs at the 20-to-25-year mark, exterior repaints, flooring, and original builder-grade windows.
cities.note: This territory is Chandler and Gilbert together. One contractor per trade covers both cities.
cities.needs_data: A geo-grid centred on a specific Gilbert subdivision would demonstrate the street-by-street effect better than any paragraph.

faqs.q: Why does work here come in waves?
faqs.a: Gilbert was built as large master-planned subdivisions over a compressed period, so whole streets reach the same replacement point within a season or two of each other. When one house re-roofs or repaints, the neighbours see it and follow. Map visibility gets you the first job on the street; the street gets you the rest.

faqs.q: My homes are newer. Is there really work here?
faqs.a: The mid-1990s and early-2000s builds are now twenty to thirty years old, which is exactly when roofs, builder-grade windows and original flooring come due together. The searches skew toward replacement and upgrade rather than emergency repair, but the volume is real and growing every year.

faqs.q: Should I target Gilbert or Chandler?
faqs.a: You do not have to choose. They are sold as a single territory, so one contractor per trade covers both.

faqs.q: How quickly could I see movement in Gilbert?
faqs.a: The honest answer is that grid points on the edge of your radius usually move first, in the first couple of months, and the centre consolidates later. Anyone promising a specific position by a specific date is guessing.

cities.hook: the least contested map in the metro.
cities.sub: Glendale has the demand of an established city and the map competition of a much smaller one. That gap is the whole opportunity.
cities.market: Glendale carries a mix most Valley cities do not: a genuinely old core with mid-century and earlier housing, large stretches of 1970s and 1980s subdivisions, and newer development pushing north and west around the sports and entertainment district. Housing age across most of the city sits squarely in the window where roofs, HVAC systems and windows all need replacing rather than repairing.
cities.why: What makes Glendale worth a territory is not the demand — it is the competition. Marketing spend in this metro concentrates east: Scottsdale, Chandler, Gilbert. West Valley profiles are consistently less complete, less reviewed and less maintained than their East Valley equivalents, which means the same work that barely moves the needle in Scottsdale can take the top three here. It is the cheapest map in the Valley to win and one of the more durable to hold.
cities.trades_why: Heat-driven and age-driven trades lead — HVAC first, then roofing, exterior paint, and garage doors.
cities.note: This territory covers Peoria as well. One contractor per trade holds both.
cities.needs_data: Run a comparison scan of the same trade in Glendale and Scottsdale — the completeness gap is the argument, and it is measurable.

faqs.q: Is the West Valley really less competitive?
faqs.a: Consistently, yes. Marketing spend in this metro concentrates east toward Scottsdale, Chandler and Gilbert, and West Valley profiles are noticeably less complete and less maintained as a result. The same work that barely registers in Scottsdale can take the top three here.

faqs.q: Does that advantage last?
faqs.a: It lasts as long as it takes competitors to notice, which historically has been years rather than months in this part of the Valley. Holding a position is also cheaper than winning it, so getting in early compounds.

faqs.q: I work across the whole West Valley, not just Glendale. Does that matter?
faqs.a: It helps, and it is worth saying so on your site and in your profile's service areas. Glendale and Peoria are sold as one territory precisely because contractors here rarely work one city.

faqs.q: What about the stadium and entertainment district traffic?
faqs.a: It has little bearing on home improvement search. What matters in Glendale is housing age, and most of the city sits squarely in the window where roofs, HVAC and windows need replacing rather than repairing.

cities.sub: Peoria runs nearly thirty miles north to south, and the contractor opportunity at one end has almost nothing in common with the other.
cities.market: Peoria is unusually long and narrow, and it behaves like two cities. The southern end is established, adjacent to the Sun City retirement communities, and full of owners who are older, equity-rich, decisive, and highly responsive to reviews and to being treated well on the phone. North Peoria is newer growth — larger homes, younger families, and a build cycle recent enough that the work is upgrade and shade rather than replacement.
cities.why: The two ends search differently and convert differently. Southern Peoria and its Sun City neighbours will call rather than fill in a form, will ask about licensing, and will tell their entire community about the experience afterwards — which makes review velocity and call handling the ranking levers that matter. North Peoria behaves like Gilbert: newer stock, subdivision waves, and searches that skew toward comfort and appearance.
cities.trades_why: Comfort trades lead — HVAC, shade and shutters, walk-in and low-threshold shower conversions, and roofing.
cities.note: This territory covers Glendale as well. One contractor per trade holds both.
cities.needs_data: Age-in-place conversions (walk-in showers, low-threshold enclosures) are a real and under-served search cluster here — worth a dedicated service page for whoever takes this territory.

faqs.q: Why does Peoria behave like two different markets?
faqs.a: Because it is nearly thirty miles long. The southern end is established and sits against the Sun City retirement communities; north Peoria is newer growth with larger homes and younger families. They search differently, they convert differently, and a profile tuned for one is not tuned for the other.

faqs.q: Are age-in-place conversions worth targeting?
faqs.a: They are one of the most under-served search clusters in this territory. Walk-in showers, low-threshold enclosures and grab-bar installation get searched steadily around the Sun City fringe and almost nobody has a dedicated page for them.

faqs.q: My customers call rather than fill in forms. Does that break tracking?
faqs.a: No, it is the reason call tracking exists. A tracking number on the profile and the site records and attributes every call, which matters more here than almost anywhere given how phone-first the southern end of the city is.

faqs.q: Is Peoria sold separately from Glendale?
faqs.a: No, they are one territory. One contractor per trade holds both.

cities.sub: Tempe cannot grow outward, so almost everything here is renovation — and a large share of the buyers are landlords, not homeowners.
cities.market: Tempe is fully built out and hemmed in on every side, which makes it the most renovation-dominated city in the metro: no new subdivisions, an ageing mid-century core, and a housing market shaped by Arizona State University. A substantial share of the single-family stock is investor-owned and rented, much of it to students, and turned over on an academic calendar rather than a homeowner's timeline.
cities.why: That changes who is searching and what wins. A landlord between tenants is not comparing craftsmanship — they need flooring, paint or a working garage door done inside a two-week window, and they will book whoever is visible and can commit to a date. Response speed and clearly stated availability outrank polish. It also means repeat business is concentrated: one property manager with a dozen doors is worth more than a dozen one-off homeowners, and they find their first contractor on the map like everyone else.
cities.trades_why: Turnover trades lead — flooring, interior repaint, garage doors, and HVAC repair on ageing units.
cities.note: Tempe sits in the Mesa & East Valley territory. One contractor per trade covers the whole East Valley.
cities.needs_data: Property-manager and multi-property enquiries are a distinct search intent worth its own page for whoever holds this territory.

faqs.q: Are landlords worth chasing as customers?
faqs.a: One property manager with a dozen doors is worth more than a dozen one-off homeowners, and they find their first contractor the same way everyone else does. What they want is different: a date you can commit to, not craftsmanship photographs.

faqs.q: Why does Tempe have so little new construction work?
faqs.a: The city is landlocked and fully built out, so almost everything is renovation. That makes the housing stock older on average than the East Valley around it and pushes demand toward replacement, turnover and repair.

faqs.q: Does the student rental market actually matter to my trade?
faqs.a: It sets the calendar. A large share of single-family stock is investor-owned and turns over on an academic timetable, which concentrates flooring, paint and door work into predictable windows. Being visible and available in those windows is most of the opportunity.

faqs.q: Which territory covers Tempe?
faqs.a: Mesa and the East Valley. One contractor per trade covers the whole East Valley including Tempe.
